problems.memo_sentence: The paper frames a derivative-pricing problem for a hypothetical quantum-money market, focusing on pricing (especially American-style) options on quantum money using numerical methods that can handle non-Gaussian, shock-driven market dynamics and stochastic volatility.
problems.source_evidence: “This paper does not address these problems in defining QM. Instead, this papaer addresses how options on such QM can be calculated.” / “When QM arrives, options on quantum markets will be required for purposes of hedging and speculation.”
problems.explanation: The memo presents the paper as broadly framing a derivative-pricing problem, but the paper is more specific: it says it does not define quantum money and focuses on calculating options on QM when/if QM arrives. The memo omits that narrower framing.

problems.memo_sentence: The quantum component is a kernel-based quantum path-integral algorithm, qPATHINT/qPATHTREE, obtained by generalizing the PATHINT path-integral code to N dimensions and converting all variables and functions to complex form to represent quantum evolution.
problems.source_evidence: “The 1-D PATHINT code was generalized by the author to N dimensions. A quantum generalization also was made to the code, changing all variables and functions to complex variables, changing about 7500 lines of PATHINT code.”
problems.explanation: The memo omits the paper’s explicit limitation that this was a large code conversion of about 7500 lines. That implementation burden is part of the paper’s methodological description and should not be dropped.

problems.memo_sentence: The authors emphasize that their "hybrid" classical–quantum workflow is currently implemented entirely on classical computers, effectively emulating the intended hybrid behavior. They argue that Monte Carlo and importance-sampling methods are not convenient for time-sequential serial random shocks, which motivates their kernel-based path-integral approach instead of classical Monte Carlo for this use case, but they do not provide explicit performance comparisons or speedups against alternative classical algorithms.
problems.source_evidence: “This project demonstrates how some hybrid classical-quantum systems may be calculated using only classical (super-)computers.” / “This project, however, concerns time-sequential serial random shocks, which are not conveniently treated with Monte-Carlo/importance-sampling algorithms.” / “The 2-D problem takes on the order of 200 times the 1-D problem.”
problems.explanation: The memo correctly notes the classical implementation and Monte Carlo limitation, but it misses the paper’s explicit scaling limitation that 2-D is about 200 times more expensive than 1-D. That is a substantive limitation of the approach.

problems.memo_sentence: For higher-dimensional systems (more than two factors), the authors recommend moving from full kernel representations to parameterized fits of drifts and covariance matrices to keep runtimes manageable.
problems.source_evidence: “When the length of time is an issue, e.g., for dimensions > 2, fits of drifts and covariance matrices to parameterized forms is a very good option [50].”
problems.explanation: The memo turns a qualified recommendation into a firmer prescription. The source frames this as a good option when runtime becomes an issue, not as a universal requirement.
